desc:
Houses and heaters stand on a line; houses and heaters list their integer positions (unsorted, duplicates allowed). Every heater warms all positions within distance r of it (so both ends are included), and all heaters use the same radius r.

Return the smallest non-negative integer r such that every house is warmed by at least one heater.

Example: houses = [1, 2, 3, 4], heaters = [1, 4]. Radius 1 warms 1-2 from the first heater and 3-4 from the second; radius 0 leaves houses 2 and 3 cold. The answer is 1.
hints: Suppose the radius is fixed. Sort both arrays. For the leftmost house, which heater is the natural one to cover it?
Keep a pointer into the sorted heaters that only moves right: skip heaters whose right reach h + r is still left of the house. The first remaining heater must also satisfy h - r ≤ house.
If a radius works, every larger radius works. Binary search r in [0, 10^9] and use the two-pointer check in O(n + m) per probe.
editorial: Sort houses and heaters. For a given r, walk through the houses from left to right with a heater pointer j. While heater j lies too far left (heaters[j] + r < house) it cannot help this house or any later one, so advance j. If no heater is left, or the current one is too far right (heaters[j] - r > house), the radius fails. Otherwise this house is warmed.

The check is monotone in r, so binary search finds the smallest working radius in O(log 109) probes of O(n + m) each, after an O(n log n + m log m) sort. A direct alternative is to compute, for every house, the distance to its nearest heater with a binary search in the sorted heaters, and take the maximum of these distances.
time: O(n log n + (n + m) log R)
